lesson.title: More Than Addresses: The Vocabulary of a DNS Zone
lesson.summary: A DNS zone is a small database of resource records, and the record type tells you what kind of question that entry answers, from a plain IP address to a mail server to a security policy.
lesson.body:
Every zone in the DNS hierarchy you just read about is really just a list of entries called resource records. Each record has a name, a type, a value, and a time to live, and the type is what tells a resolver what kind of question the record answers. People often talk about DNS as if it only maps names to addresses, but a real zone file carries several distinct kinds of information side by side.

The most familiar types are A and AAAA. An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address, something like example.com pointing to 192.0.2.10. An AAAA record does the same job for IPv6, mapping a hostname to a 128 bit address such as 2001:db8::10. They answer the most basic DNS question there is: what address do I connect to for this name.

A CNAME record is different. It does not point to an address at all, it points to another name. If www.example.com has a CNAME pointing to example.com, a resolver that looks up www.example.com has to notice the CNAME and then go look up example.com's own A or AAAA record to finish the job. This is useful when you want one name to simply follow another, but it comes with a real restriction: a name that has a CNAME cannot have any other record type alongside it, and you generally cannot put a CNAME at the very top of a zone, because the zone apex needs its own NS and SOA records.

An MX record answers a completely different question: where should mail addressed to this domain be delivered. MX records point to a mail server's hostname and carry a priority number, and lower numbers are preferred. A domain might have mail.example.com at priority 10 as the primary mail server and backup-mail.example.com at priority 20 as a fallback that only gets used if the first one cannot be reached.

An NS record answers yet another question: which name servers are authoritative for this zone. This is the record type that actually implements the delegation described in the hierarchy chapter, and it is central to how both root name servers and authoritative servers do their jobs, which the next few chapters cover directly.

Finally, a TXT record just holds arbitrary text. It looks like a catch all, and it is, but in practice it is used for very specific machine readable purposes, most commonly proving ownership of a domain to some outside service, or publishing an anti spoofing email policy such as an SPF string like v=spf1 include:_spf.example.com ~all.

Put together, a small real zone for example.com might contain an A record pointing to 192.0.2.10, an AAAA record pointing to 2001:db8::10, a CNAME sending www.example.com to example.com, two MX records for mail.example.com and backup-mail.example.com, NS records naming ns1.example.com and ns2.example.com as authoritative, and a TXT record carrying that SPF string. Six very different questions, six different record types, one small zone.
